new_bank_questions.title: Which measurements can the events distinguish?
new_bank_questions.body: Let Ω={a,b,c,d} and F={∅,{a,b},{c,d},Ω}. Is X with values (2,2,3,3) measurable? Is Y with values (0,1,0,1) measurable? Exhibit a threshold event for each answer.
new_bank_questions.answer: X is measurable: for 2≤t<3, {X≤t}={a,b}, with ∅ below 2 and Ω at or above 3. All are in F. Y is not measurable: for 0≤t<1, {Y≤t}={a,c}, which is not in F. The same four numerical outcomes can support one measurement but not the other because F distinguishes only the two blocks.

new_bank_questions.title: A transformed uniform measurement
new_bank_questions.body: On Ω=(0,1) with Borel events and uniform probability, let X(ω)=ω and W=X². Explain why W is measurable, then compute P(W≤1/4) and P(1/4<W≤9/16).
new_bank_questions.answer: The square function is continuous, hence Borel measurable; its composition with X is measurable. Since ω is positive, {W≤1/4}=(0,1/2], whose probability is 1/2. Also {1/4<W≤9/16}=(1/2,3/4], whose probability is 3/4−1/2=1/4. These are probabilities of inverse-image events, not areas under a guessed density.
